summary: `Buffer::to_original` and `Buffer::as_flat` deserialize a sending process's bytes with `rkyv::access_unchecked`, and the root position rkyv transmutes at is derived from the message `offset` the same sender chooses, so any process can hand any server it can name an archived value whose relative pointers and lengths it controls.
explanation: `from_memory_message` sets `used` from `mem.offset` verbatim and `slice` from the mapped page length, relating them nowhere; `to_original` then evaluates `rkyv::access_unchecked::<U>(&self.slice[..self.used])`, and rkyv computes the root as `size.saturating_sub(size_of::<Archived T>())` over that slice. rkyv's own documentation states the bytes must already represent a valid archived type and names `access` as the validating alternative, which is not called anywhere in the tree; the only bounds assertion rkyv carries is `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` and is absent from release builds. The kernel copies `offset` and `valid` through unchanged and its `lend_memory` never sees them. Reachability needs no grant: the name server has a hardcoded well-known id, and it plus PDDB register with an unlimited connection count that checks a count rather than an identity.
malicious_actor: a process already running on the device, with no privilege of its own
parameter: the lent page's bytes plus offset (MemoryMessage, IPC)
trigger_flow: hostile process -> Message::Borrow with attacker bytes and attacker offset -> kernel syscall.rs copies offset through -> server calls Buffer::from_memory_message -> to_original::<T>() -> rkyv::access_unchecked at a sender-chosen root position -> rkyv::deserialize follows the archived type's relative pointers
malicious_input_example: map one page, fill it with chosen bytes rather than an rkyv serialization, then xous::send_message(cid, Message::Borrow(MemoryMessage { id, buf: page, offset: MemoryAddress::new(0x40), valid: MemorySize::new(0x1000) }))
